Long COVID Basics For Everyone May 6, 2026 Español Key points Long COVID is a serious illness that can result in chronic conditions, require comprehensive care, and can sometimes cause disability. Long COVID can include a wide range of ongoing symptoms and conditions that can last months to years after COVID-19 illness. Anyone who had a SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus that causes COVID-19, can experience Long COVID, including children. Following core strategies to lower your risk of severe COVID-19 illness is the best way to prevent Long COVID. Living with Long COVID can be difficult and isolating, especially when there are no approved tests that can determine if your symptoms or conditions are due to Long COVID and there are no approved treatments. About Long COVID Long COVID is defined as a chronic condition that occurs after SARS-CoV-2 infection and is present for at least 3 months. Long COVID includes a wide range of symptoms or conditions that may improve, worsen, or be ongoing. Talk to your healthcare provider if you have symptoms that last for months after an infection. Long-Duration Energy Storage Background From providing critical backup power during natural disasters to supporting more renewable energy coming online, energy storage technologies make the grid more flexible and resilient. Today’s energy storage technologies are not sufficiently scaled or affordable enough to meet energy demand that fluctuates throughout the day and night. Long-duration energy storage (LDES) is a cost-effective option to increase grid reliability and resilience so that reliable, affordable electricity is available whenever and wherever to everyone. DOE defines LDES as storage systems capable of delivering electricity for 10 or more hours in duration. Program Overview The Long-Duration Energy Storage portfolio helps to advance LDES systems toward widespread commercial deployment. The goal of this portfolio is to fund projects that will overcome the technical and institutional barriers that exist for deployment, with a focus on different technology types for a diverse set of regions. Looking for a Minor League Baseball team to cheer for next season? Why not root for the underdog? These franchises, scattered across six leagues and four levels of play, need your support as they attempt to purge the losing demons of decades past. Isn’t it time they won it all? Minor League Baseball is a world in flux, so the teams on this list may have changed their name, affiliation, league or level of play over the course of the drought in question. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published November 12, 2026 Look low in the northeastern sky on an autumn evening, and you might spot something unusual: a bright star flashing red, green, and blue. That’s Capella, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. But despite appearances, the star isn’t actually changing colors. The dazzling display is an optical effect caused by starlight passing through Earth’s atmosphere. And Capella isn’t the only star that puts on this kind of show. “Stars appear to twinkle or shimmer in the night sky, but this is not an inherent trait of stars,” says Emily Watson, astrophysicist and planetarium supervisor at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center. “As the light from a star passes through different densities and temperatures within our atmosphere, the light bends in a process called refraction.” The color flashes happen because Earth’s atmosphere bends different wavelengths of light by different degrees. Story and video by Kinsey Gidick Published May 15, 2026 When considering a trip to Baja, it’s nearly impossible to dodge the words of two famous men: Jacques Cousteau and John Steinbeck. The pioneering French oceanographer famously called the Gulf of California “the aquarium of the world.” Not surprisingly, that line shows up everywhere—typed into brochures and slipped into itineraries, hovering like a promise. Once again, Piniella -- the longtime great manager -- is one of eight candidates on the Contemporary Baseball Era ballot for managers, executives and umpires, announced last week. A 16-member panel consisting of Hall of Fame players, Major League executives, media members and historians will consider each of the eight candidates, who must receive a minimum of 12 votes (at least 75%) to be elected. The results of the Class of 2027 ballot will be announced on Sunday, Dec. 6. Joining Piniella is some very steep competition of fellow managers and baseball executives. The list includes Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner and Bill White.​ Piniella, 83, has come painfully close to election on two previous occasions only to fall one vote shy -- both times -- from getting the long-awaited call from Cooperstown. During a Major League managerial career with five clubs that spanned 23 seasons, Piniella posted a record of 1,835-1,713. He is ranked 17th all-time in wins. Of the 16 managers ahead of him, 12 are in the Hall of Fame. Two of those managers are Baker and Bochy. Piniella managed the Yankees (1986-88), Reds (1990-92), Mariners (1993-2002), Devil Rays (2003-05) and Cubs (2007-10). He has led his clubs to seven postseason appearances and helmed eight seasons of 90 or more victories with four different clubs. A tall, soft-spoken man, he was nevertheless one of the loudest and most respected voices in his field. During his twenty-five years of fieldwork in Northwest Alaska, Giddings worked on five major excavations. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Lower Sonoran Field Office The BLM Lower Sonoran Office manages 1.4 million acres of public land in south-central Arizona, including the half-million acre Sonoran Desert National Monument , located 60 miles southwest of Phoenix. The monument contains biologically diverse national communities, including large Saguaro cactus forests and contains many significant archaeological and historic sites. In an effort to rehabilitate damage from off-highway vehicles, access to about 20 percent of the monument has been temporarily closed to motorized use. Public lands within this field office are near developed and expanding communities and are heavily used. The lands are managed for multiple use and provide diverse recreational opportunities, mining, wildlife habitat, grazing, and wilderness, all overlaying a rich cultural past. The field office oversees six wilderness areas, four Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, the Juan Bautista de Anza National Historic Trail and one property listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It brings an end to one of the most successful athlete-coach partnerships in the history of Irish sport after 12 years together. Carson, a former gymnast, helped assist McClenaghan to Olympic gold on the pommel horse at the 2024 Games in Paris in what was Ireland's first gymnastics medal. Together, they completed gymnastics' 'Grand Slam'. McClenaghan, 27, also won back-to-back World Championship golds, as well as three European and a Commonwealth title on top of their Olympic success. Carson has parted company with Gymnastics Ireland, where he was high performance coach and in charge of the Olympic programme for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles. Lyme Disease Surveillance and Data For Everyone Sept. 9, 2026 Key points CDC monitors Lyme disease through national case surveillance and other data sources. More than 80,000 Lyme disease cases are reported to CDC each year. An estimate using insurance claims suggests 476,000 people are treated for Lyme disease each year. Surveillance data explained More than 80,000 Lyme disease cases are reported to CDC each year by states and jurisdictions. Lyme disease became a nationally notifiable condition in the United States in 1991. Case reports of Lyme disease are routinely collected and verified by state and local health departments in accordance with their legal mandate and surveillance practices. Cases are then classified according to the national surveillance case definition developed by the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE). After information that could identify a person is removed, selected case information is shared with CDC through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) . pages.text: Major baseball awards effects on Hall of Fame chances Skip to Content Winning a Baseball Writers' Association of America Award is an achievement in and of itself, a tangible testament to a well-played season. When a player wins MVP, Cy Young or Rookie of the Year, he’s already added to his resume, which might one day help him become enshrined in Cooperstown. But not every player to win an MVP, Cy Young or Rookie of the Year Award is in the Hall of Fame. Of the 122 Major League players in the Hall of Fame who retired in 1956 or later -- the first year of the Cy Young Award, the newest of the BBWAA player awards -- 53 never won a BBWAA Award. It’s not a prerequisite, but it definitely helps. So, where does the distinction lie? What percentage of players to win multiple such awards are in the Hall of Fame? Rookie of the Year is typically the least predictive of future greatness, simply because we can’t give more weight to players with multiple awards the way we can with MVP or Cy Young, since a player can win only once. Of the 87 Rookie of the Year winners who have already been eligible to be on the Hall of Fame ballot, just 19 are in the Hall of Fame. However, it is worth noting that of those 87 HOF ballot-eligible Rookie of the Year winners, just 21 won at least one more BBWAA Award in their careers. Of those 21, 11 are in the Hall of Fame. We can’t track players to win multiple Rookies of the Year, but that’s a way to look at multi-award winners that include ROYs. pages.text: Mammals Made By Viruses | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Mammals Made By Viruses By Carl Zimmer Published February 14, 2012 • 6 min read If not for a virus, none of us would ever be born. In 2000, a team of Boston scientists discovered a peculiar gene in the human genome. It encoded a protein made only by cells in the placenta. They called it syncytin. The cells that made syncytin were located only where the placenta made contact with the uterus. They fuse together to create a single cellular layer, called the syncytiotrophoblast, which is essential to a fetus for drawing nutrients from its mother. The scientists discovered that in order to fuse together, the cells must first make syncytin. What made syncytin peculiar was that it was not a human gene. It bore all the hallmarks of a gene from a virus. Viruses have insinuated themselves into the genome of our ancestors for hundreds of millions of years. They typically have gotten there by infecting eggs or sperm, inserting their own DNA into ours. There are 100,000 known fragments of viruses in the human genome, making up over 8% of our DNA. Most of this virus DNA has been hit by so many mutations that it’s nothing but baggage our species carries along from one generation to the next. Yet there are some viral genes that still make proteins in our bodies. Syncytin appeared to be a hugely important one to our own biology. Originally, syncytin allowed viruses to fuse host cells together so they could spread from one cell to another. Now the protein allowed babies to fuse to their mothers. Photograph: US Department of Justice/PA US news Man armed with axe accused of destroying US military plane at Shannon airport in Ireland Daithi O’Corrain charged with destruction of US government property, after allegedly smashing gauges and cutting hydraulic lines Nadeem Badshah Tue 17 Nov 2026 19.06 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 19.58 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks. O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland , according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan. He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.
